place.zh: 沂中医 · 体育场 · 九月

setup.zh: 入学第十二天，体测一千米。沈芒当着半个看台的女生，跑死在第四百米上，吐在一个女孩递来的塑料袋里。第二天他在篮球队的报名表上签了字；周一头一回训练，叫马小宝扣坐在视频里那个红圈上。
setup.en: Twelfth day of term, the 1000-metre fitness test. In front of half a stand of girls Shen Mang dies at four hundred metres and throws up into a plastic bag a girl hands him. The next day he signs the basketball team's form; at Monday's first practice Ma Xiaobao dunks him onto the red circle from the video.

recap.zh: 一千米四分五十八，没及格，吐了；签了篮球队的表；红圈里坐了一回；称了体重：五十九点六，体脂二十一点四，罚球十投一。
recap.en: Four fifty-eight on the thousand, failed, threw up; signed the team form; sat once in the red circle; weighed in: fifty-nine point six, twenty-one point four percent, one of ten from the line.

zh: 一只白球鞋，一个小本子。
en: A white sneaker, a small notebook.

story.zh:
入学第十二天，[沈芒]{注=jin-shenmang}当着半个看台的女生，跑死在了一千米的第四百米上。

说「死」，未免夸张；可在他自己看来，一个字也不夸张。嗓子眼里像塞了一把烧红的铁砂，两条腿是别人借给他、这会儿正急着要回去的。他张大了嘴喘，又快又浅，一口刚吸到喉咙，下一口已经急着出来，两口气在嗓子眼里撞个满怀，谁也不肯让谁。

一分钟以前，他还跑在第二。哨子一响他就冲了出去——他怕的倒不是一千米，是看台，女生组正坐在那儿等着跑八百。头一百米风从耳朵边上刮过去，看台上有人指着这边说了句什么，他心里烧得厉害：沈芒啊沈芒，原来你是个跑步的天才，十八年没人发现，连你自己都没发现。

两百米过线，终点上报了一声「三十九」，他心里一乐。然后，腿先沉了，像有人往他裤腿里各灌了一袋沙子；跟着是一股酸，从腿肚子往上爬；跟着是喘。三百米，眼镜从左边过去了，路过还腾出一口气：「忙哥，保重。」四百米，老蔡从右边过去了，拍了拍他的肩：「我先走一步。」他想回一句「你走好」，嘴张开，出来的只有一口热气。

此人姓沈，名芒，十八岁，沂州中医药大学针灸推拿学专业大一新生；学校在山东临沂城北，沂河西岸。若问他有什么特长：话多。这会儿，一个字也说不出来了。

到六百米，所有人都从他身边过去了。最后超过他的那一位，一路跑一步、停一步，还有工夫跟看台上的人挥手。沈芒眼睁睁看着那个背影远去，脸上一阵一阵地烧，比腿还烧：倒数第一的经验他有的是，可当着全院女生的面拿，这是头一回。剩下最后一百米，他不知道哪儿来的一口气，咬着牙，竟又跑快了一点。

终点线上，体育部的[雷老师]{注=jin-lei}按停秒表，像念一张罚单：「沈芒，四分五十八。及格线四分三十二。九月二十四号补测。」

沈芒膝盖一软便要往地上蹲，雷老师一把薅住他的后领子：「别蹲！走！」走了没几步，胃里翻江倒海。一只手往他手里塞了个塑料袋：「吐这里。跑道明天还要用。」

是个女孩的声音，不高，不急。他弯下腰，「哇——」的一声，把中午那碗牛肉面原原本本还给了这个世界，吐得眼泪鼻涕一齐下来。眼前一阵一阵发黑，黑里头恍恍惚惚坐着他太奶，在老家院子的小板凳上冲他招手：「芒啊，来，饺子刚出锅。」他太奶走了六年了。他心想：完了，这是来接我了，我才十八，饺子我还不想吃。

等那阵黑过去，他只看见一双白球鞋、一截蓝色的志愿者马甲、一只攥着小本子的手。那声音在头顶上说：「今年头一个。」笔尖在本子上沙沙记了一笔。

他最怕的，就是这一笔。他提着一袋自己的午饭，腿软得只想坐，到底没坐，一步一步把那一圈走完了。走着走着，他想的不是那一千米，是那个本子：她在上头，记了我一笔什么？

那天夜里，六一七宿舍开了一场批斗会。

被批斗的人躺在下铺，两眼望着上铺的床板。报到那天他把三栋楼各爬了一遍六层才找着这间屋，屋里从此管他叫「沈忙」；他自己管那叫熟悉校园。上铺的[老蔡]{注=jin-laocai}举着手机，把年级群里一段视频放了第三遍——不知谁从看台上拍的，配着一行字：「论一个人可以把一千米跑得多么有层次」。视频里他先冲在第二，跟着一个一个地被超过，像一块叫潮水慢慢冲到岸上的木头。[眼镜]{注=jin-yanjing}说：「停。最后一百米，他是不是又快了一点？」老蔡说：「快了。」眼镜说：「回光返照。」两个人笑得从床上滚下来。沈芒也想笑，一笑，吐空了的肚子先抽了一下。

笑完了，眼镜扶了扶眼镜，手机屏幕一亮，脸色变了：「沈忙，学生手册上写着，体测不到五十分，只发结业证，没有毕业证。」沈芒一头栽进了枕头里。枕头里闷了半天，他翻过身来看墙。墙上贴着两张纸，一张课表，眼镜拿红笔在周四上午第一节上圈了一圈：针灸推拿学导论；一张是迎新礼包里送的二十四节气挂图，眼镜贴的，说学中医的，墙上没这个不像话。

老蔡探出头：「你作文写得那么好，怎么跑来学中医了？」沈芒道：「调剂的。第六个志愿是我妈填的。」他说这话时，眼睛看着那幅挂图，没看人。

眼镜从桌上拿起一本图书馆的旧书，《抱朴子内篇》——医古文老师在群里开了一张课外书单，全班只有他当真去借了。他一字一顿地念：「[夫人在气中，气在人中。]{典=baopu-zhili}」念完抬眼看他，「你吐进袋子的是面条。气吐不进去——真吐干净了，那叫断气。」沈芒道：「那我今天离断气，也就差一个塑料袋。」

他又问：「哎，给我递塑料袋那个女生，哪个学院的？」老蔡道：「看见了。你吐的时候，人家在旁边记数。记吐了几个。全年级四百多号人跑完了都在那儿喘，就你一个吐了。」沈芒道：「……那我这算独一份。」

十点，他妈打来视频。不知哪位家长热心，把看台上拍的那段转进了新生家长群。「你爸看了八遍。」他爸的大脸「呼」地挤进镜头，两个鼻孔占了半个屏幕，郑重其事：「芒啊，跑不过，就走。走，不丢人。我当年体测，就是走完的。」他妈道：「倒数第二。」他爸道：「倒数第一那个，是抬下去的。」说完往后一靠，「哎哟」一声，又若无其事：「车座子硬。」他妈道：「膝盖。刚从日照跑回来，十一个钟头。」镜头一晃，扫到他爸一条腿架在板凳上，护膝缠得像个粽子。他爸道：「这叫护膝。开车的勋章。」

半夜他饿醒了，借着路灯，指头在挂图上找到芒种——他是芒种那天生的——往前挪一格：小满。底下一行小字：「麦粒渐饱，尚未全满。」

「小满，」他小声念，「还没满。听着像个永远吃不饱的。」

肚子咕噜一声，替小满答应了。

第二天中心广场百团大战，他是去棋社的——查过了，下棋全程坐着。一百多个摊位从图书馆门口一直摆到食堂，街舞社放着音乐，药膳社发酸梅汤，推拿社的学长举着喇叭喊「免费试按，不疼不要钱」，后头一个试按的人正在惨叫。他往里挤，半路被一面手写的横幅挡住：「校篮球队 · 招新」。

摊位边上立着一个可移动的篮架，一个人正在扣篮。这人站着像一堵墙，跳起来像一堵飞起来的墙，一米九几，脚上一双沈芒在网上看过价钱、又默默关掉页面的球鞋。他扣一个，围观的女生叫一声；扣到第十几个，落了地，接过一只大摇杯，喝一口奶白的蛋白粉，气都不怎么喘。沈芒看着他，心里很不服气：同样是人，我跑一千米差点把肺吐出来，他蹦了十几下跟没事人一样，这不公平。

折叠桌后头坐着一个马尾辫的女孩，面前摊着那个小本子。

这个声音他认得。从看见她的脸，到拿起报名表，一共三秒；有一秒半是在找笔。

她翻到一页，念道：「沈芒。前两百米三十九秒，全组第二；四百米，第十；最后一个过线。吐了。」抬眼，「头两百米是欠着氧气跑的。欠了要还，所以停下来还喘半天。」

原来那一笔记的是这个。他的耳朵烧了起来。

一堵墙晃了过来，手腕上一块表，手里一只大摇杯，歪头看他的报名表：「沈芒。芒硝的芒？泻药。我们家药房里，芒硝放最底下那一排，便宜。」伸出一只锅盖似的手，「[马小宝]{注=jin-maxiaobao}。中药学大三。家里开药房的，三十几家。以后你开了方子，来我家抓药，给你打折。小意思。」这话说得随随便便，倒像在说今天天气不错。沈芒握了握那只手，觉得自己握住的不是手，是一个承诺：这辈子，你都打不过我。

马小宝转头对她道：「阿禾，这种你也收？咱们招的是队员，不是吉祥物。」

她叫[阿禾]{注=jin-ahe}。沈芒脑子一热，话就出来了：「他扣十几个气都不喘，我跑个一千米差点把命跑没了。同样是两条腿，他那两条是原装的，我这两条是赠品？」马小宝笑出了声，拿下巴朝阿禾一指：「问她。运动康复的，教练都听她的。」阿禾没笑，像在答一道答过很多遍的题：「腿是原装的。是心肺没练过。练过的人，肉里烧氧气的东西多，心一下送出去的血多。他早上醒来躺着，心跳五十几。你多少？」沈芒低头看手环，开学前他妈网上买的，九十九块：八十八。阿禾道：「站着、说着话的，不算。明早醒了，躺着量。」他再低头一看，又蹿上去了。他把手环往袖子里塞了塞——这东西太诚实。

她递给沈芒一个球：「投一个。」球比他想的沉，也比他想的大。他学着电视里的样子屈膝，抬手，脑子里过了一遍他看过的所有比赛，出手。球飞得很高，很有信心，越过篮筐，越过篮板，不偏不倚，砸翻了马小宝的摇杯，半杯蛋白粉淌在他的球鞋上。沈芒僵在原地，脑门上的汗一颗一颗往下掉。马小宝低头看了看，笑了：「没事。一双鞋。」擦得很慢，「家里还有。」

沈芒觉得，他这辈子没听过比这更吓人的「没事」。

旁边一个大一的大高个刚签完名，看了一眼这阵势，搁下笔，转身往街舞社的摊子去了。她在本子上记：「刘一鸣，一米八八。跑了。」马小宝乐了：「大刘跑了，来了个小沈。」

「篮球队收人，看两样：能不能练，肯不肯来。」她不理他，「能不能练，我不知道；肯不肯来——你吐完了，没坐下，自己走完了那一圈。我那会儿在记吐的人数，顺便看见的。」她指了指最底下一栏，「本人签字。」

沈芒签了，签得比高考那张答题卡还用力。他念了十二年书，得过的唯一一张奖状是小学三年级的「进步奖」，上头连名次都没有；这张表上只有一行字，是他的。他把它又看了一眼，才递过去。阿禾把表压在那一沓空表的最上面——那一沓表，一张也没写过。

马小宝拍了拍他的后背，拍得他往前一冲：「恭喜啊，今年招新的头名。说不定也是最后一名。周一早上六点，球馆。我亲自带你热身。」说罢跳起来又扣了一个，篮架晃了三晃。阿禾头也没抬：「别理他。平常校队一块儿练；到了院系杯，各回各的学院——他回中药学院，你回针推。队友变对手，在那儿。」

夜里，她发来一张表，「沈芒 · 补测前十四天」，一条一条：每天早上慢跑二十分钟，边跑边能说整句话；不许空腹跑，早饭鸡蛋一个，队里出；十二点前睡；周一早上六点球馆照来，三千米先别跑；末一条：「补测那天，前两百米不许快过四十五秒。你是死在前两百米上的。」底下另起一行：「鸡蛋一个一块二，十四天，十六块八，记在你名下。」

沈芒回：「过了有奖吗？」对面回：「看你补测成绩。」

十二点，一个陌生号码：「我，马小宝。」跟着一段视频——他在球馆里扣篮，篮底下坐着一个人，叫扣得一屁股坐在地上，拿红圈圈出来，旁边写着：上一个新人。视频底下一行字：「周一早上，你站这个位置。」

九月十四日，周一，开课第一天。凌晨五点四十，六一七黑得像一口锅。沈芒睁着眼躺了十分钟，两根指头按在腕子上，对着秒表数了一分钟：七十六。他把这个数在心里念了三遍，生怕起了床就忘了。

球馆门口，阿禾蹲在台阶上，脚边一只保温袋。她递过来一个煮鸡蛋，还热着：「不许空腹跑。」沈芒剥着蛋壳：「这算第几个？」「第四个。表从体测那天数起，十四天。前两天你没吃着，照记。」「没吃着也记？」「表是十四天的。」他把蛋整个塞进嘴里，噎得直瞪眼。这一个还没咽下去，账上已经是四个了。

天刚蒙蒙亮，全队在红跑道上跑三千米，他一个人在最外道跑他的二十分钟。边跑边能说整句话——这是规矩。说什么好呢？周四要默写十二正经，他昨晚抄了一张纸揣在兜里，便一边跑一边念：「手太阴肺经。手阳明大肠经。足阳明胃经。足……足……」马小宝从他身边超过去，回过头来：「他跟谁说话呢？」队长邢斌道：「跟自己。」马小宝道：「练嘴？那他全队第一。」

雷老师掐着秒表站在弯道上，等他挪过来：「你念叨什么呢？」「十二正经。」雷老师愣了一愣。他带了二十年队，见过跑着跑着哭的、吐的、唱歌的，跑着念经的，头一回。他想了想，没骂，伸手指了指他的嘴：「念得出整句，就是速度对了。接着念。」

跑完了回球馆，分组打半场。马小宝把球在手心里掂了两掂，往沈芒怀里一塞：「来，你持球，我防你。」沈芒运了两下，第三下球便弹进了马小宝手里。马小宝一转身，两步，起跳——沈芒脑子里只剩下一个念头：那个红圈。

他没躲。不是勇敢，是来不及。

一堵墙从天上压下来，球砸进篮筐，篮架嗡嗡地晃，沈芒一屁股坐在了地板上，坐的正是视频里那个位置，分毫不差。四下里一阵哄笑。马小宝落了地，伸出一只锅盖似的手把他拉起来：「站得挺准。」又压低了嗓子，往场边一瞥，「你是为她来的吧？」

沈芒道：「我那是在练卡位。」

「卡位？」马小宝也看场边，阿禾正低着头写字，「卡她的位？」说罢拍拍他的肩，走了。

歇口气的工夫，队群里多了一条视频——刚才那一扣，已经有人发出来了，红圈换了个人圈着，底下马小宝回了一行：「这一个新人。」沈芒把手机扣在大腿上，觉得全馆的人都在看他：看他坐在地上，也看他往场边看的那一眼。他正想找条地缝，场边那个声音不高不急地喊：「沈芒。过来，称一称。」

器材室里一台体重秤，一把钳子模样的东西。秤上的数字刚停，一只大脚伸过来，脚尖在秤沿上轻轻一踩，数字往上一蹿。马小宝倚在门框上：「给你添两斤，看着体面点。」阿禾头也不抬：「脚拿开。」数字落回去：五十九点六。阿禾记下，看了马小宝一眼：「秤是准的。你那两斤，记你账上。」马小宝笑了一声，晃着摇杯走了。

「这是皮褶卡钳。捏一捏皮下有多厚，算体脂。」她捏他胳膊后头，捏他肩胛骨底下，捏他肚子旁边。沈芒怕痒，捏一下抖一下，抖到第三下，阿禾道：「再抖，就按抖的算。」他便不抖了。她按了一会儿计算器：「百分之二十一点四。你这个体重，不少。瘦，可是没什么肉，油倒是有一点。」

沈芒低头看了看自己。他十八年来一直以为自己是瘦，原来是瘦子里的胖子——好比一个人一直以为自己穷，一查，还欠着钱。

最后是罚球，十个，进一个。阿禾合上本子：「周四默写，背了吗？去年这一回，白卷十一张。」又翻出一张通知：「十月十七，校队试训，三项：体能、力量、技术。过了，算校队的人；不过，这一行就划掉。你今天这几个数，三项里一项也过不了。」

「称这个，有什么用？」他问，「称完了，我还是我。」

「不称，你练了一个月，不知道是长了还是掉了。」阿禾道，「秤上的数不好看，不要紧。要紧的是，下一回它跟这一回不一样。」
story.en:
On his twelfth day at university, in front of half a stand full of girls, Shen Mang died at the four-hundred-metre mark of the thousand-metre run.

"Died" is an exaggeration; to him it wasn't one by a single word. His throat felt stuffed with a fistful of red-hot iron grit, and his legs were on loan from someone who wanted them back right now. He gasped with his mouth wide open, fast and shallow, each breath barely reaching his throat before the next shoved its way out, two breaths colliding in his windpipe and neither giving way.

A minute earlier he had been running second. He had shot off at the whistle — it wasn't the thousand metres he feared, it was the stand, where the girls were waiting to run their eight hundred. For the first hundred metres the wind tore past his ears, someone in the stand pointed this way and said something, and his chest burned with it: Shen Mang, oh Shen Mang, you were a running genius all along — eighteen years and nobody found out, not even you.

At the two-hundred line the finish called out "thirty-nine", and his heart leapt. Then his legs went heavy, as if someone had poured a bag of sand down each trouser leg; then an ache climbed from his calves; then the gasping. At three hundred Glasses went past on his left, sparing a breath: "Hang in there, Mang." At four hundred Old Cai went past on his right and patted his shoulder: "I'll go on ahead." He wanted to answer "safe travels"; his mouth opened and only hot air came out.

His name is Shen Mang, eighteen, a first-year in Acupuncture and Tuina at Yizhou University of Chinese Medicine, north of Linyi city in Shandong, on the west bank of the Yi River. His one talent: he talks a lot. Right now he could not get out a single word.

By six hundred everyone had passed him. The last to go by jogged a step and walked a step and still had breath to wave at the stand. Shen Mang watched that back recede, his face burning in waves, hotter than his legs: he had plenty of experience of coming last, but coming last in front of the whole faculty's girls was a first. With a hundred metres left he found a breath from somewhere, clenched his teeth, and actually sped up a little.

At the finish line Mr Lei from the PE department stopped his stopwatch and read it out like a parking ticket: "Shen Mang, four fifty-eight. Pass mark four thirty-two. Retest on September the twenty-fourth."

Shen Mang's knees gave and he started to squat; Mr Lei hauled him up by the back of his collar: "Don't squat! Walk!" A few steps on, his stomach heaved. A hand pushed a plastic bag into his: "In here. The track's in use tomorrow."

A girl's voice, not loud, not hurried. He bent double and, with a great "hwaa", returned his lunchtime beef noodles to the world, tears and snot coming out together. Blackness came in waves, and in the blackness sat his great-grandmother on the little stool in the courtyard back home, beckoning: "Mang, come on, the dumplings are just out of the pot." His great-grandmother had been dead six years. He thought: that's it, she's come to collect me, I'm only eighteen, I don't want dumplings yet.

When the black passed he saw only a pair of white trainers, a strip of blue volunteer's vest, and a hand holding a small notebook. The voice above his head said: "First one this year." A pen scratched a line into the notebook.

That line was what he feared most. Carrying a bag of his own lunch, legs begging to sit, he didn't sit; step by step he walked the full lap out. And as he walked it wasn't the thousand metres on his mind but the notebook: what had she written about him?

That night Room 617 held a struggle session.

The accused lay on the bottom bunk staring at the slats above. On registration day he had climbed six floors in each of three buildings before finding this room, and the room had called him "Shen Busy" ever since; he called it getting to know the campus. From the top bunk Old Cai held up his phone and played a clip from the year group for the third time — someone had filmed it from the stand and captioned it "How many layers can one man put into a thousand metres". In it he led in second, then was passed one by one, like a log the tide nudges slowly onto the beach. Glasses said: "Pause. The last hundred — did he speed up again?" Old Cai said: "He did." Glasses said: "Last flicker of the candle." The two of them laughed themselves off their beds. Shen Mang wanted to laugh too; one laugh and his emptied stomach cramped first.

When the laughing was over Glasses pushed up his glasses, his phone screen lit, and his face changed: "Shen Busy, the student handbook says: below fifty in the fitness test, you get a completion certificate, not a degree." Shen Mang buried his head in the pillow. After a long while muffled in it he rolled over and looked at the wall. Two sheets were pinned there: a timetable, with Thursday's first period circled in red by Glasses — Introduction to Acupuncture and Tuina; and a chart of the twenty-four solar terms from the welcome pack, Glasses's too, who said a medical student's wall without one was a disgrace.

Old Cai poked his head out: "You write such good essays — what are you doing studying Chinese medicine?" Shen Mang said: "Got reassigned. The sixth choice was my mum's." As he said it his eyes were on that chart, not on anyone.

Glasses picked up an old library book from the desk, the Inner Chapters of the Baopuzi — the medical classics lecturer had posted a reading list to the group, and he was the only one in the class who had actually gone and borrowed from it. He read it out syllable by syllable: "Man is in qi, and qi is in man." He looked up. "What you threw up in that bag was noodles. Qi can't be thrown up — throw all of it up and that's called expiring." Shen Mang said: "Then I was one plastic bag short of expiring today."

Then he asked: "Hey — the girl who handed me the bag. Which faculty?" Old Cai said: "Saw her. While you were throwing up she was next to you counting. Counting how many threw up. Four hundred-odd in the year ran, all of them standing there panting, and you were the only one who threw up." Shen Mang said: "...So I'm one of a kind."

At ten his mother video-called. Some keen parent had forwarded the clip from the stand into the new first-years' parents' group. "Your dad's watched it eight times." His father's big face swooped into the frame, two nostrils filling half the screen, solemn: "Mang. If you can't run it, walk it. Walking's no disgrace. When I did my fitness test, I walked it." His mother said: "Second to last." His father said: "The one who came last was carried off." He leaned back with an "ow", then, as if nothing had happened: "Hard seat." His mother said: "Knees. He just drove back from Rizhao, eleven hours." The camera swung and caught his father's leg up on a stool, a knee brace wound round it like a rice dumpling. His father said: "That's a knee brace. A driver's medal."

In the night he woke up hungry and, by the streetlight, found Grain in Ear on the chart with his finger — he was born on Grain in Ear — and moved one square back: Grain Buds, Xiaoman. A small line beneath it: "The grain swells but is not yet full."

"Xiaoman," he murmured. "Not full yet. Sounds like someone who never gets enough to eat."

His stomach growled, answering for Xiaoman.

The next day was the clubs fair on the central square, and he was heading for the chess club — he'd checked: chess is played sitting down the whole way through. A hundred-odd stalls ran from the library doors to the canteen; the street-dance club had music going, the medicinal-cuisine club was handing out sour plum drink, a senior from the tuina club was shouting through a loudhailer "free trial massage, no pain no pay", while the person being trialled behind him screamed. He pushed inward and halfway along was blocked by a hand-lettered banner: "University Basketball Team · Recruiting".

Beside the stall stood a portable hoop, and someone was dunking on it. Standing, the man was a wall; jumping, a flying wall; one metre ninety-something, in a pair of trainers Shen Mang had once looked up online and then quietly closed the page on. He dunked, and the watching girls shrieked; after a dozen he landed, took a big shaker bottle of milky protein powder, drank, and was barely out of breath. Shen Mang watched him, deeply aggrieved: we're both human — I nearly coughed my lungs up over a thousand metres, and he bounces a dozen times like it's nothing. It isn't fair.

Behind the folding table sat a girl with a ponytail, that small notebook open in front of her.

He knew the voice. From seeing her face to picking up the form took three seconds; a second and a half of that was spent looking for a pen.

She turned to a page and read: "Shen Mang. First two hundred, thirty-nine seconds, second in his heat; at four hundred, tenth; last across the line. Threw up." She looked up. "The first two hundred, you ran on borrowed oxygen. Borrowed has to be repaid — that's why you were still panting long after you stopped."

So that was what the line said. His ears caught fire.

A wall drifted over, a watch on his wrist, a big shaker in his hand, head tilted at the form: "Shen Mang. Mang as in mangxiao? That's a laxative. In our pharmacies it goes on the bottom shelf, cheap." He stuck out a hand the size of a pot lid. "Ma Xiaobao. Third-year, Chinese Pharmacy. Family's in pharmacies — thirty-odd. When you start writing prescriptions, come to us to fill them, you'll get a discount. Easy." He said it as casually as remarking on the weather. Shen Mang shook the hand and felt he had taken hold not of a hand but of a promise: you will never, in this life, beat me.

Ma Xiaobao turned to her: "Ahe, you take this sort too? We're recruiting players, not a mascot."

Her name was Ahe. Shen Mang's brain overheated and the words came out: "He dunks a dozen times without panting, and I nearly died over a thousand metres. Same two legs — his are the original parts and mine are the free gift?" Ma Xiaobao laughed aloud and jerked his chin at Ahe: "Ask her. Sports rehab. Even the coach listens to her." Ahe didn't laugh; she answered as if it were a question she'd answered many times: "The legs are original. The heart and lungs are untrained. In a trained person the muscle has more of the stuff that burns oxygen, and the heart sends out more blood per beat. He wakes up lying in bed with a pulse in the fifties. What's yours?" Shen Mang looked at his wristband — ninety-nine yuan, bought online by his mother before term: eighty-eight. Ahe said: "Standing and talking doesn't count. Tomorrow morning, when you wake, lying down." He looked again and it had climbed. He tucked the band up his sleeve — the thing was too honest.

She handed Shen Mang a ball: "Take a shot." It was heavier than he expected, and bigger. He bent his knees the way they did on TV, raised his arms, ran every game he had ever watched through his head, and released. The ball flew high and full of confidence, over the rim, over the backboard, and landed exactly on Ma Xiaobao's shaker, knocking it over; half a bottle of protein ran onto his trainers. Shen Mang froze, sweat dropping bead by bead from his forehead. Ma Xiaobao looked down, then smiled: "It's nothing. One pair of shoes." He wiped them slowly. "There are more at home."

Shen Mang felt he had never in his life heard a more frightening "it's nothing".

A first-year beanpole beside them had just signed; he took one look at the scene, put down the pen, and turned for the street-dance stall. She wrote in the notebook: "Liu Yiming, one eighty-eight. Ran." Ma Xiaobao was delighted: "Big Liu ran, little Shen came."

"The team takes people on two things: can you be trained, and will you turn up." She ignored him. "Whether you can be trained, I don't know. Whether you'll turn up — you finished throwing up, didn't sit down, and walked the lap out yourself. I happened to see it while I was counting the ones who'd been sick." She pointed at the bottom box. "Sign here."

Shen Mang signed, pressing harder than on his college entrance answer sheet. In twelve years of school the only certificate he had ever won was a "Most Improved" in year three, with no place on it; on this form there was a single line, and it was his. He looked at it once more before handing it over. Ahe laid it on top of the stack of blank forms — a stack no one else had written on.

Ma Xiaobao slapped him on the back hard enough to pitch him forward: "Congratulations, first name on this year's list. Maybe the last. Monday, six a.m., the gym. I'll warm you up personally." He jumped and dunked again, and the hoop rocked three times. Ahe didn't look up: "Ignore him. The university team trains together; for the faculty cup you go back to your own faculties — he to Chinese Pharmacy, you to Tuina. Teammates become opponents there."

That night she sent him a chart, "Shen Mang · fourteen days to the retest", item by item: twenty minutes' easy jog every morning, slow enough to speak whole sentences; never run on an empty stomach, one egg for breakfast, on the team; in bed by midnight; Monday six a.m. at the gym as usual, skip the three thousand; and last: "On the day, the first two hundred no faster than forty-five seconds. You died in the first two hundred." On a new line below: "Eggs one yuan twenty each, fourteen days, sixteen eighty, on your account."

Shen Mang replied: "Any prize if I pass?" The reply: "Depends on your retest time."

At midnight, an unknown number: "Me, Ma Xiaobao." Then a video — him dunking in the gym, and under the hoop someone knocked flat onto his backside, circled in red, with the caption: the last new recruit. Under the video, a line: "Monday morning, you stand here."

September 14th, Monday, first day of classes. At five forty in the morning Room 617 was as black as the inside of a pot. Shen Mang lay awake for ten minutes, two fingers on his wrist, counting a minute against the stopwatch: seventy-six. He said the number to himself three times, afraid he'd forget it the moment he got up.

At the gym door Ahe was squatting on the step with a thermal bag at her feet. She handed him a boiled egg, still warm: "No running on an empty stomach." Shen Mang peeled it: "Which one is this?" "The fourth. The chart counts from the day of the test, fourteen days. You didn't get the first two; they count anyway." "Even ones I didn't eat?" "The chart is fourteen days." He pushed the whole egg into his mouth and nearly choked, eyes bulging. This one wasn't even swallowed and the account already said four.

In the first grey light the whole team ran three thousand on the red track while he jogged his twenty minutes alone in the outside lane. Slow enough to speak whole sentences — that was the rule. Speak what? Thursday's dictation was the twelve regular channels; he had copied them onto a sheet the night before and had it in his pocket, so he jogged and recited: "Lung channel of hand-Taiyin. Large Intestine channel of hand-Yangming. Stomach channel of foot-Yangming. Foot... foot..." Ma Xiaobao overtook him and looked back: "Who's he talking to?" Xing Bin, the captain, said: "Himself." Ma Xiaobao said: "Mouth training? Then he's first on the team."

Mr Lei stood on the bend with his stopwatch and waited for him to shuffle up: "What are you muttering?" "The twelve channels." Mr Lei paused. Twenty years coaching teams, he'd seen people cry while running, vomit while running, sing while running; chant scripture while running was a first. He thought about it, didn't shout, and pointed at his mouth: "If you can get a whole sentence out, the pace is right. Keep chanting."

Back in the gym afterwards they split into half-court groups. Ma Xiaobao weighed the ball in his palm a couple of times and shoved it into Shen Mang's arms: "Here, you've got the ball, I'm on you." Shen Mang dribbled twice; on the third the ball bounced into Ma Xiaobao's hands. Ma Xiaobao spun, two steps, and rose — and in Shen Mang's head there was room for one thought only: the red circle.

He didn't dodge. Not courage — no time.

A wall came down out of the sky, the ball slammed through the hoop, the stand hummed, and Shen Mang sat down hard on the floor, in the exact spot from the video, not an inch off. Laughter all round. Ma Xiaobao landed and pulled him up with a pot-lid hand: "Good positioning." Then, lower, with a glance at the sideline: "You're here for her, aren't you?"

Shen Mang said: "I was practising boxing out."

"Boxing out?" Ma Xiaobao looked at the sideline too, where Ahe was writing with her head down. "Boxing her out?" He patted his shoulder and went off.

While they caught their breath, a video appeared in the team group — that dunk, already posted, the red circle now round a different man, and Ma Xiaobao's reply under it: "This new recruit." Shen Mang laid the phone face down on his thigh, feeling the whole gym watching him — watching him sit on the floor, and watching the glance he had sent at the sideline. He was looking for a crack in the floor to crawl into when that voice called, not loud, not hurried: "Shen Mang. Over here. Weigh in."

In the equipment room stood a scale and a thing like a pair of pliers. The number had just settled when a large foot came over and pressed lightly on the rim, and the number jumped. Ma Xiaobao leaned on the door frame: "Adding a kilo for you, so it looks respectable." Ahe didn't look up: "Foot off." The number fell back: fifty-nine point six. Ahe wrote it down and gave Ma Xiaobao a look: "The scale is accurate. Your kilo goes on your account." Ma Xiaobao laughed once and ambled off with his shaker.

"These are skinfold calipers. They pinch the fat under the skin to work out body fat." She pinched the back of his arm, under his shoulder blade, beside his belly. Shen Mang was ticklish and flinched at each pinch; on the third Ahe said: "Flinch again and I'll record the flinch." He stopped flinching. She tapped a calculator: "Twenty-one point four percent. For your weight, that's not low. Thin, but not much muscle, and a bit of fat."

Shen Mang looked down at himself. For eighteen years he had thought he was thin; it turned out he was the fat kind of thin — like someone who always thought he was poor and then finds out he's in debt as well.

Last came free throws: ten, one in. Ahe closed the notebook: "Dictation Thursday — have you learned them? Last year, eleven blank sheets." She turned up a notice: "October seventeenth, university-team trials, three events: fitness, strength, skills. Pass and you're on the team; fail and this line gets crossed out. On today's numbers you wouldn't pass any of the three."

"What's the point of weighing all this?" he asked. "Weighed or not, I'm still me."

"If I don't, you train a month and have no idea whether you've gained or lost." Ahe said. "The numbers on the scale being ugly doesn't matter. What matters is that next time they're different."

exits.means: goes on to the first week of classes
